subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 68-year-old man has had 6 months of progressive low back pain and now reports severe pain after a minor fall. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. Skeletal radiographs reveal multiple well-circumscribed punched-out lytic lesions in the skull and spine, and serum protein electrophoresis shows a narrow M spike.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
Multiple myeloma
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
Myelodysplastic syndrome
Metastatic bone disease from an occult solid tumor

explanation_correct: This patient has the classic CRAB features of multiple myeloma: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, and Bone lytic lesions with back pain and pathologic fractures. A monoclonal plasma cell clone overproduces a single immunoglobulin, producing the M spike, and its cytokines drive osteoclast-mediated bone destruction. The disorder occurs in older adults, and peripheral smear may show rouleaux formation.

explanation_incorrect.A: MGUS produces an M spike but has fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells and lacks all CRAB findings and lytic lesions; this patient is symptomatic.
explanation_incorrect.C: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia overproduces IgM and causes hyperviscosity, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly rather than punched-out lytic lesions.
explanation_incorrect.D: Myelodysplastic syndrome causes cytopenias with maturation defects and fewer than 20% marrow blasts, not a monoclonal paraprotein or lytic bone lesions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Metastatic cancer can cause painful bone lesions but does not produce an M spike, Bence Jones proteinuria, or the cytokine-driven hypercalcemia seen here.

educationalObjective: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia of older adults defined by CRAB findings, a monoclonal M spike, and punched-out lytic bone lesions.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with multiple myeloma has a serum calcium of 12.9 mg/dL with a suppressed parathyroid hormone level. Bone biopsy shows increased numbers of osteoclasts immediately adjacent to clusters of monoclonal plasma cells, and radiographs show multiple lytic lesions.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the hypercalcemia in this patient?

options.text: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide secretion acting on osteoblasts
Increased renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity producing excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Accelerated osteoblastic new bone formation with secondary calcium release
Cytokine secretion (eg, IL-1, TNF-alpha, RANK-L) by malignant plasma cells increasing osteoclast activity
Phosphate retention from renal failure driving calcium deposition into bone

explanation_correct: Malignant plasma cells secrete cytokines such as IL-1, TNF-alpha, and RANK-L that markedly increase osteoclast activity. The resulting bone resorption releases calcium into the circulation and produces the characteristic punched-out lytic lesions. This mechanism is local and cytokine driven, which is why parathyroid hormone is suppressed rather than elevated.

explanation_incorrect.A: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia is characteristic of humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy from squamous cell tumors, not multiple myeloma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase is seen in granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, not in myeloma.
explanation_incorrect.C: Myeloma produces osteolytic rather than osteoblastic lesions; the problem is unopposed resorption, not new bone formation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Renal insufficiency can aggravate hypercalcemia, but phosphate retention with calcium deposition would lower, not raise, serum calcium and is not the primary mechanism.

educationalObjective: Myeloma hypercalcemia results from plasma cell cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha, RANK-L) that activate osteoclasts and cause lytic bone destruction.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 65-year-old man with IgG multiple myeloma has a routine urine dipstick that is negative for protein. A 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis, however, demonstrates a large monoclonal light-chain band, and immunofixation confirms urinary monoclonal free light chains.
question: Which of the following best explains the negative routine urine dipstick despite heavy light-chain proteinuria?

options.text: The dipstick is primarily albumin sensitive and does not detect immunoglobulin light chains
Light chains are completely reabsorbed and metabolized by renal tubules so none reach the urine
Immunoglobulin light chains are too large to be filtered across the glomerulus
The alkaline buffer of the dipstick denatures Bence Jones proteins before detection
Concurrent renal insufficiency raises the concentration threshold required for a positive dipstick

explanation_correct: The urine dipstick detects albumin, not immunoglobulin light chains. Bence Jones proteinuria from free monoclonal light chains therefore gives a negative dipstick, and urinary involvement must be confirmed with urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation. These light chains are also directly nephrotoxic and contribute to the renal insufficiency of myeloma.

explanation_incorrect.B: Light chains are freely filtered and do appear in the urine in large amounts when production exceeds tubular reabsorption, so they are not completely metabolized.
explanation_incorrect.C: Light chains are small proteins that filter freely; it is larger proteins such as albumin that are normally retained by the glomerulus.
explanation_incorrect.D: The dipstick reagent is specific for albumin; there is no pH-dependent destruction of Bence Jones proteins involved in the false-negative result.
explanation_incorrect.E: Renal failure changes excretion but not dipstick chemistry; the discrepancy here is due to the type of protein, not the glomerular filtration rate.

educationalObjective: Bence Jones light-chain proteinuria is missed by the albumin-based urine dipstick and requires urine electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with back pain, anemia, and renal insufficiency has a serum M spike. Serum immunofixation identifies a single monoclonal immunoglobulin class. Her physician discusses which paraprotein is most typical of this disease.
question: Which immunoglobulin class is most commonly overproduced in multiple myeloma?

options.text: IgD
IgM
IgG
IgE
IgA

explanation_correct: Multiple myeloma most commonly overproduces IgG, followed by IgA and then light chains only. This hierarchy is a classic distinguishing point: an IgM monoclonal protein instead suggests Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, in which the large pentameric IgM causes hyperviscosity.

explanation_incorrect.A: IgD myeloma is a rare variant and is not the most common immunoglobulin class in this disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: IgM overproduction characterizes Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, where the large IgM molecule produces hyperviscosity symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgE myeloma is extremely uncommon and is not the classic paraprotein of multiple myeloma.
explanation_incorrect.E: IgA is the second most commonly overproduced immunoglobulin in myeloma, after IgG.

educationalObjective: The monoclonal immunoglobulin in multiple myeloma is most often IgG, then IgA, then light chains alone.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 66-year-old man has an asymptomatic IgG M spike of 1.8 g/dL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and no bone lesions. Bone marrow biopsy shows 6% monoclonal plasma cells. Six months later he develops back pain and multiple lytic lesions.
question: Which of the following initial marrow findings would have supported a diagnosis of multiple myeloma rather than MGUS?

options.text: Fewer than 10% plasma cells in a reactive polytypic marrow
Increased megakaryocytes with loose clustering
At least 20% myeloblasts with Auer rods
More than 10% lymphoplasmacytic cells with intranuclear inclusions
More than 10% monoclonal plasma cells with clock-face chromatin and intracytoplasmic immunoglobulin inclusions

explanation_correct: Multiple myeloma is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing more than 10% monoclonal plasma cells with characteristic clock-face chromatin and intracytoplasmic inclusions containing immunoglobulin. MGUS has fewer than 10% monoclonal plasma cells, an M spike below 3 g/dL, and no CRAB findings. Rouleaux formation on peripheral smear is another clue to a plasma cell dyscrasia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Fewer than 10% polytypic plasma cells in a reactive marrow supports MGUS or a reactive process, not myeloma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Clustered megakaryocytes suggest a myeloproliferative neoplasm rather than a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.
explanation_incorrect.C: Myeloblasts with Auer rods indicate acute myelogenous leukemia, not a plasma cell dyscrasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lymphoplasmacytic cells with intranuclear IgM inclusions are the hallmark of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

educationalObjective: More than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells with clock-face chromatin and cytoplasmic immunoglobulin inclusions distinguishes myeloma from MGUS.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with IgG multiple myeloma develops progressive nephrotic-range proteinuria and symptoms of restrictive cardiomyopathy over several months. Renal biopsy shows amorphous eosinophilic deposits that stain positively with anti-light-chain antiserum and show apple-green birefringence with Congo red.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new cardiac and renal disease?

options.text: Deposition of intact IgM pentamers within vessel walls
Secondary amyloidosis derived from serum amyloid A protein
Direct infiltration of the myocardium and kidney by monoclonal plasma cells
Primary (AL) amyloidosis from deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains
Uric acid crystal deposition caused by tumor lysis syndrome

explanation_correct: Primary AL amyloidosis is a well-known complication of multiple myeloma. Monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains misfold and deposit as amyloid in the kidney, heart, tongue, and soft tissues, producing nephrotic syndrome and restrictive cardiomyopathy. The light-chain staining and Congo red birefringence on biopsy confirm the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Intact IgM pentamers cause hyperviscosity in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, not Congo red-positive amyloid deposits.
explanation_incorrect.B: Serum amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis is secondary to chronic inflammation or infection and is not driven by a monoclonal plasma cell clone.
explanation_incorrect.C: Direct malignant plasma cell infiltration is not the mechanism here; the biopsy shows amorphous extracellular light-chain deposits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tumor lysis with uric acid crystals causes acute kidney injury, not chronic amyloid deposition with restrictive cardiomyopathy.

educationalObjective: Multiple myeloma can cause primary AL amyloidosis, in which monoclonal light chains deposit as amyloid in kidney and heart.
